extracted.intended_audience: general magazine readers interested in journalism, media ethics, and legal/professional consequences
extracted.subtask_description: A long-form magazine feature exploring the Stephen Glass journalism-fraud scandal and the subsequent moral-character litigation over his attempts to become a lawyer; discusses standards used to judge rehabilitation, candor, and trustworthiness. Useful for understanding how journalism ethics and bar-admission determinations are evaluated in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-checking annotation key
rubrics_metrics.description: The key at the top of this page indicates that phrases underlined in blue have been confirmed as true; phrases underlined in red have been confirmed to be untrue; phrases underlined in pencil cannot be confirmed either way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to annotate Stephen Glass’s past articles after the scandal; subsequent pages are described as 'very, very red' (i.e., many confirmed falsehoods).

rubrics_metrics.name: What constitutes journalistic fabrication
rubrics_metrics.description: Fabrication consisted of making up characters, scenes, events, whole stories from first word to last; creating fake interview notes, fake business cards, and fake voicemails; inventing details (e.g., a convention of Monica Lewinsky memorabilia, fake quotes about politicians).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the article underscore both petty and serious fabrications (funny trinkets vs. racist or career-damaging quotes). The piece emphasizes extreme lengths taken to hide fabrications, making them particularly egregious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial responsibility / verification standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and fact-checkers are responsible for verification; suspicion and active verification (e.g., pressing for details, physically checking locations) are critical to catching fabrications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Chuck Lane’s role: his skepticism and insistence on verifying the location of a supposed hackers’ convention ultimately exposed Glass’s lies. The article contrasts charm vs. rigorous checking as an editorial anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bar admission moral-character requirement (burden to prove rehabilitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant must demonstrate that he 'is no longer the same person who behaved so poorly in the past' — i.e., prove rehabilitation and present moral character adequate for admission to the bar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The California Supreme Court rejected Glass’s admission on the ground that he failed to meet this standard; the standard is framed as the applicant’s burden to prove reformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full disclosure and candor to bar authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants must fully disclose past misconduct and be candid with bar examiners and prior bar applications; failing to disclose or misleading the bar is a significant negative factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A deciding factor against Glass was discovery that he had misled the New York bar about how much he’d worked with magazines to help detect his fabrications and that he added articles to his list as late as the 2010 trial — conduct that undermined his credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of evidence considered in moral-character hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence reviewed includes testimony from witnesses (family, colleagues, employers, professors, psychiatrists), records of therapy, steady employment and job duties, acts of contrition (apologies), and demonstrable work helping others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article lists 22 witnesses who testified for Glass (girlfriend, judge, law professors, psychiatrists, colleagues) and cites therapy frequency, steady employment at a law firm, and client-service work (e.g., securing a settlement for a homeless client) as the kinds of proof offered in support of rehabilitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divergent judicial conceptions of rehabilitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Lower courts may view rehabilitation as 'moving on' from the original crime and living a reformed life; higher courts (as characterized here) may expect an oncological approach—rooting out every trace and demonstrating meticulous engagement with the past wrongdoing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article contrasts the lower courts' acceptance of a quieter, lived reformation with the state Supreme Court’s expectation of rigorous, demonstrable remediation, noting the author’s sympathy with the lower-court view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of candid, comprehensive confession as indicator of reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Some evaluators expect a 'full, voluntary, unrestrained, uninhibited, generous, forthcoming confession' and detailed admissions of wrongdoing as central evidence of genuine reform and trustworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted demands (from Chuck and court attitudes) emphasize that partial or self-serving accounts undermine credibility; lingering omissions about the extent of fabrications harm the applicant’s case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer practice for reintegrating someone with past misconduct (client-disclosure protocol)
rubrics_metrics.description: An employer may require the reformed employee to disclose past misconduct proactively to clients and to use that disclosure as a tool to build trust and encourage client candor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paul Zuckerman’s firm has Glass tell clients upfront that he 'worked at a magazine and he lied, made up stories, and got caught' so clients learn of the history on the firm’s terms; the practice is justified as promoting full truth-telling with vulnerable clients, though the article also raises concerns about potential manipulation or performance.
